newsitem.title: USA: Qian says China no threat, assures on Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Qian says China no threat, assures on Hong Kong.

text.p: Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen offered assurances on Tuesday that China would not replace the Soviet Union as "the main threat" to America and Hong Kong would retain much autonomy under Beijing control.
Appearing before a U.S.-China business group, Qian predicted a U.S.-China accord on peaceful nuclear cooperation could be finished in time for a fall summit in Washington.
He repeated Beijing's denials that China made political donations to U.S. election campaigns, as has been alleged, and said China attaches "great importance to human rights."

He also promised China would open its markets wider, as the United States has demanded, and he urged negotiators to redouble efforts for an agreement on China's bid to join the World Trade Organisation.

Qian, in Washington for top-level talks that include a meeting with President Bill Clinton on Wednesday, went out of his way to try to allay American sceptics who challenge the wisdom of Clinton's effort at greater engagement with Beijing.
He criticised unnamed Americans who are "spreading the China threat theory (which argues that) China has replaced the former Soviet Union as the main threat to the United States."
"These views could not be more wrong," he said.

"China does not have a tradition of expansion...(its) defence policy is completely defensive in nature...Even if it becomes stronger ... China will not pursue aggression and expansion, still less will it seek hegemony," Qian said.

As for Hong Kong, which reverts from British to Chinese control on July 1, he said: "The Hong Kong SAR (special administrative region) will enjoy a high degree of autonomy, including the executive power, legislative power and independent judicial power and the power of final trial."

The United States has grown increasingly concerned about Hong Kong as the changeover draws near, with many critics complaining that prepartory steps by Beijing are eroding the colony's tradition of democracy and basic freedoms.
Martin Lee, Hong Kong's leading pro-demoracy activist, was in Washington last week urging the Americans to strongly press Beijing to preserve Hong Kong's rights and freedoms.
Qian, however, insisted the "degree of autonomy enjoyed by Hong Kong is unmatched in the world."
On the peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement, Qian said: "I believe the agreement can be launched before the time of the meeting of the leaders of the two countries."
One of his tasks was to prepare for a fall summit in Washington between Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin.

The nuclear agreement, which could give Beijing access to millions of dollars worth of American-made computers, was signed in 1985 but never implemented because of U.S.concerns about China's nuclear cooperation with rogue states like Iran.

Last year, as part of a deal in which Beijing promised not to help unsafeguarded nuclear programmes, the two sides agreed to try to implement the pact. But Beijing has not put in place a nationwide system of exports control, a key U.S. demand.

Washington supports Beijing's bid to join the World Trade Organisation but, given China's growing economy and huge U.S. trade surplus, has insisted it be accomplished on acceptable commercial terms, not the easier terms Beijing argued for.
Qian told the business group: "China will open its markets still wider and increase its imports from the United States."
He also called for U.S. and Chinese negotiating teams to "redouble efforts" to reach an agreement on WTO membership.
He said the annual U.S. debate over renewing favourable trade benefits for China harms bilateral ties.

The United States has repeatedly expressed concerns about China's sale of missiles and other weapons technology to Iran and Pakistan. Qian insisted such concerns are "unfounded" and said Beijing's approach to conventional weapons sales has been "prudent" and "responsible."
